learners._comment: What the learner is CALLED. A pupil at school and a student at university are the same thing in the tree and different in the prose, so a tree picks one with the `learner` config row - and only the key goes in tree.csv. The inflected forms live here, because inflection is something that varies with language, and a teacher building their own tree should not have to write grammar in a spreadsheet. `leadIn` is the line the panel puts in front of the description: a skill is a verb phrase ("The student can: add two ..."), a concept is a definition, so the two need different lead-ins. A tree that needs a word not listed here costs one more entry in this file - not a change to the engine.

help.label: How do I use this page?
help.heading: How do I use this page?

sections.heading: The menu button
sections.body: Press the ☰ button at the bottom left, next to this help button, to open a menu with the back link, light/dark mode, your progress and the other buttons on the page — explained below.

sections.heading: The map
sections.body: The map shows how skills and concepts build on one another, from the most basic on the left to the most composite on the right. Boxes you do not have the prerequisites for yet appear grey and locked — tick off the ones you are missing first. Drag to pan the map, and use +/- or the mouse wheel to zoom.

sections.heading: Click a box
sections.body: When you click a box you get the prerequisites, a full description of the learning goal, and an AI instruction you can copy and paste into an AI chat to practise that particular skill. Mark the box as mastered when you know it — your progress is saved in your browser, and you can remove the mark again whenever you like.

sections.heading: “Show all learning goals”
sections.body: This button gives you a single systematic list of every learning goal in the course, sorted by topic — useful when you want an overview or want to read the whole list without clicking through the map. Each goal shows its status: ✓ means you have marked it as mastered, ◇ means you have everything you need to learn it now, and ⊘ shows which goals you should take first (with their code, e.g. C1).

sections.heading: “Search”
sections.body: The search looks in the name, the description and the topic of every learning goal, and marks where the word occurs. It is the quickest way into the map when you remember a word from a learning goal but not which topic it sits under. Click a result to go to the node.

sections.heading: “Build a lesson plan” (for teachers)
sections.body: At the bottom of “Show all learning goals”, teachers can tick the learning goals the next lesson should cover, set the length of the lesson, and get an AI instruction for a complete lesson plan: a starter, a walkthrough using the example-problem pair model, diagnostic questions and retrieval practice at the end. The mastery ticks are your own, in your own browser — they show what you personally have been through, not what the class actually knows.

sections.heading: “Make a test from mastered skills”
sections.body: This button gives you an AI instruction for a test covering a selection of what you have already marked as mastered. Paste it into an AI chat to test yourself across several skills at once.

sections.heading: The aid tag
sections.body: The tag on a box shows which aid level the skill belongs to — for example "Part 1" or "Part 2". If it is split into several colours, the skill belongs to several levels, and you should be able to manage it under the most restrictive one. Click the tag to open "About the course", where each level is explained.

sections.heading: “Why should I learn this?”
sections.body: This button gives you an AI instruction for a short conversation about why the subject is worth learning at all. Paste it into an AI chat if you need a nudge in the right direction.

prompt._comment: The fallback language layer. A tree whose language has no languages/<code>.json yet falls back to this file for the UI, but NOT for outputLanguage — the engine generates that from the tree's own `language` field, so a German tree converses in German on day one with no translation work. `writingStyle` is necessarily empty here: it holds examples in a specific language, and this file serves every language that has no file of its own. The language-independent half of that advice is NOT missing — it lives in prompts/shared.json → writingStyleGeneral and applies to every tree regardless. NOTE: `outputLanguage` says which language the conversation STARTS in — it must not forbid the student from asking for another one. The student's right to ask for a different language, and what happens when they do, is language-independent and lives in prompts/shared.json → languageSwitch. Do not write an absolute prohibition here: the two would contradict each other, and the model follows the prohibition.
prompt.outputLanguage: Conduct this entire conversation in {conversationLanguage}. Everything quoted from the skill tree below — node names, descriptions, prerequisites — is written in {conversationLanguage}, and that is the language {learnerDefinite} expects to be addressed in. Do not drift into another language on your own initiative, and do not comment on the language these instructions are written in. Address {learnerDefinite} as "you", and where the role has to be named, the word is “{learnerDefinite}” — not another word for the same thing.
